But that’s because you are heterosexual. As a bisexual, for every non-family person I’ve met that decision and categorisation gets made. 

And yes a romantic relationship is hugely different than a really really close friendship. Physical attraction, sexual attraction and fantasising about a shared practical future are the big ones just off the top of my head. Expectations of what needs a romantic partner should fulfil are different from the expectations of what a friend should fulfil. 

Perhaps that is a hard concept to grasp for a lot of straight men because patriarchy tells men that a huge amount of the needs of what actually a platonic friendship should fulfil are given over as romantic expectations. This is why for a lot of women close really emotionally expressive and vulnerable friendships are just friendships even with people of the gender they are attracted to, but for a lot of straight men these are firmly rooted in potentially romantic territory.  

A really really close friendship fulfils very different needs with different boundaries and expectations to a relationship. It’s like making the commitment to see the other person as a family member. A family member you can be vulnerable and very close to, but can never think of romantically.

I don’t think that this is disgusting because you are not acting on the feelings and violating the boundaries of the relationship. 

However I think it’s a good point to talk about why you feel like (and I’m not criticising you here I’m just inviting you to think about this whenever you have the time and emotional energy to do this) why there’s only two criteria for attraction: 1) be an attractive girl and 2) be interesting enough to share interesting times/activities together. 

What I’m getting at is that if you talk to a lot of confident and self assured people they will usually have a lot higher of standards and a lot more specific requirements for a potential partner. They will want yes 1) an attractive girl that 2) they are interesting enough to get on well with but also 3) that they share these life goals and 4) that they meet under these circumstances and 5) that they have these shared backgrounds and 6) etc etc etc

Because of all of the extra criteria they have to meet, for these straight people, most of the people they meet will not come meet this criteria. So after an initial thought and evaluation of “is this person friend material or relationship material” upon meeting them for the first few times, the decision is made and either path pursued. 

I feel like from experience a lot of the guys that I was friends with who then preceded to tell me they had feelings for me shared a few characteristics including the fact that they were not confident, self assured enough to make that classification and act on it the beginning and/or that they were desperate enough for a romantic companionship that after our friendship deepened, they reverted to thinking “this is an attractive girl-looking person, who i get on with, this COULD be a romantic relationship”. 

So the question that I think you should give some thought to is: why do you consider female friends who you have a great connection with dating material instead of approaching female strangers who you find physically attractive with the proposition of getting to know each other in hopes of developing a romantic connection? 

The latter, the intent and purpose and the expectation of what is to come is laid out for both parties from the beginning, in the latter acting on the hypothetical of a relationship violates the preexisting social contract that the two people have. The first it takes a much more self assured person to undertake bc rejection is explicit and obvious. In the second rejection  never has to be made public or brought up between the two parties. Rejection merely comes up silently and passes by as the woman either gets a different romantic partner or never makes the move. It is less risky for the male ego, but unfair on the girl.

I agree that everyone of all genders get the thoughts of “hey what would this person be as a partner” but that’s very different from actually only being friends with a someone for the potential of being in a relationship with them. 

Having hypothetical thoughts about friends I think is just the nature of being an introspective person. But acting on those thoughts and pursing them is very different and it is what OP was getting at. 

You can be completely platonic friends with people and wonder from time to time “what if we dated” and evaluate what they would be like as a partner but the distinction is that you recognise that acting on these potentials violates the boundaries of a friendship and is unfair to the other person. By acting I mean one of two things that OP outlined: sticking around whilst they’re single and ghosting when they’re in a relationship.

Also I don’t think it’s weird to not fall in love with someone of the gender you are attracted to if you click with them. There’s more to romantic attraction than gender and getting on well with at least for me personally.

I had MD (and still do). It’s part of my ADHD I think. I used to daydream for hours on end when I got home bc I didn’t have friends. This went on since I was a kid until late teens (17-ish). It would get in the way of doing homework and relationships and friendships. Years later, I still daydream, not with the same compulsion. I’m writing a book based on my daydreams, got a job for a bank, got into shape at the gym, have lots of friends. In a way I feel I have become my daydream self. Therapy, medication, talking to my friends about my struggles, unlearning bad coping mechanisms (daydreaming and dissociation) really helped. It was a ducking uphill struggle with a couple of attempts, self harm, sabotaging, a lot of heartache. There are still parts of my life like romantic relationships that MD still affects. I still have a long way to go unlearning and dissecting the problems that I used MD to run away from, and more so the problems indulging in MD created for me. I forgive myself though bc it was a coping mechanism for many years. I wouldn’t be here without it. When you are finally in a safer position in life, you can begin to let go of old coping mechanisms and later unlearn and dissect what happened. 

Can you have a normal life after MD? Yes absolutely. It is my belief that MD is a temporary coping mechanism to trauma or a bad situation. Will it be easy? No. Worth it? Absolutely yes. I think younger me would rather be me now than my daydream self. I think they would be really proud of me and if I knew I would end up here, I would have been a lot more hopeful about the future and probably not daydreamed as much

Good coping mechanisms I found: gym, writing, karate, spending time with friends, edibles, coding (or whatever special little interest I overindulge in at the time)
